clinicalPearls: Type 3 (mixed) RTA combines proximal bicarbonate wasting with a distal defect in urinary acidification, so the acidosis tends to be more severe than either isolated form.

The classic inherited cause is carbonic anhydrase II (CA II) deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder producing the triad of osteopetrosis, renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification (Guibaud-Vainsel or marble brain syndrome).
Carbonic anhydrase II is expressed in both proximal and distal tubular cells, in osteoclasts and in the brain, which explains the combined renal, skeletal and neurological phenotype.
Osteopetrosis arises because osteoclasts cannot acidify their resorption lacunae, giving dense but brittle bones prone to fracture, cranial nerve compression and marrow encroachment.
A transient developmental form of mixed RTA occurs in infants owing to tubular immaturity and usually resolves with growth; the label 'type 3' is now rarely applied to adults.
Cerebral calcification, typically of the basal ganglia and periventricular regions, with developmental delay and cognitive impairment is characteristic of the CA II-deficient form.
Both a raised fractional excretion of bicarbonate and an inability to maximally lower urine pH can be demonstrated, reflecting the dual tubular lesion.
Dental anomalies, growth retardation and visual or hearing impairment from narrowing of bony foramina may accompany the syndrome.
reference.pathophysiology: Carbonic anhydrase II catalyses the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to carbonic acid and is central to hydrogen ion and bicarbonate handling in several tissues. In the proximal tubule its loss impairs reclamation of filtered bicarbonate, producing bicarbonate wasting, while in the distal nephron it limits the generation of protons required for maximal urinary acidification; the coexistence of these lesions yields a mixed pattern with features of both proximal and distal RTA. The same enzyme deficiency cripples osteoclasts, which depend on acidification of the sealed resorption zone to dissolve bone mineral, so bone turnover falls and the skeleton becomes abnormally dense yet mechanically weak, causing fractures and encroachment on marrow and cranial foramina. In the central nervous system enzyme deficiency is associated with progressive intracranial calcification and neurodevelopmental impairment. The autosomal recessive CA2 gene defect therefore unites nephrocalcinosis-sparing acidosis, osteopetrosis and cerebral calcification within a single disorder, whereas the separate transient infantile form reflects physiological immaturity of tubular bicarbonate handling rather than a fixed genetic lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited osteopetroses (for example TCIRG1 or CLCN7 forms) without renal tubular acidosis
Idiopathic basal ganglia calcification and other causes of cerebral calcification such as hypoparathyroidism
Other skeletal dysplasias with generalised osteosclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Blood gas and serum electrolytes confirming a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis
Urine pH and urinary acidification testing together with fractional excretion of bicarbonate
Skeletal survey demonstrating generalised osteosclerosis or osteopetrosis
Cranial computed tomography to detect basal ganglia and periventricular calcification
Red-cell carbonic anhydrase II activity assay
Assessment of growth, neurodevelopment, vision and hearing
redFlags: Recurrent fractures occurring despite radiologically dense bones
Progressive developmental delay or cognitive decline with intracranial calcification
Cranial nerve deficits such as visual loss, facial weakness or deafness from bony foramen compression
Severe acidosis with growth failure in infancy
reference.prognosis: The inherited CA II-deficient form is a lifelong disorder in which alkali therapy corrects the acidosis and may support growth, but the osteopetrosis, fracture tendency and neurological impairment persist and vary in severity; the transient infantile form resolves with maturation.
pitfalls: Labelling a patient as 'type 3' without recognising the underlying carbonic anhydrase II deficiency and its systemic features.
Missing osteopetrosis because dense bones remain silent until a fracture or nerve compression occurs.
Attributing cerebral calcification to hypoparathyroidism without checking calcium and parathyroid status.
Forgetting that the bones are fragile despite their increased radiographic density.
Focusing on the skeletal disease while overlooking the readily treatable acidosis.
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
